Indefinite Integration — JEE Main revision guide

Differentiation asks for the rate of a function. Indefinite integration goes backwards: the rate is given, and we look for a function that has that rate.

Source difficulties before studying

The official integration unit includes antiderivatives of fundamental functions, substitution, parts, partial fractions and trig identities, together with standard rational and radical forms.

  • Q6: the keyed formula works separately for x>0x>0x>0 and x<0x<0x<0, but is undefined and jumps at 000. The original integrand is smooth there. We explain this and give a smooth all-real answer too.
  • Q11: the printed sec⁡−1x\sec^{-1}xsec−1x match needs x>1x>1x>1 under the usual principal-value convention. For negative inputs, use the corrected domain-aware primitive.

These are source qualifications, not changes to the printed questions. Preserve domain information; a familiar formula without its conditions can have the wrong sign.

Concept C01 — What does an indefinite integral return?

If F′(x)=f(x)F'(x)=f(x)F′(x)=f(x) on an interval, FFF is an antiderivative, also called a primitive, of fff. The indefinite integral means the whole family:

∫f(x) dx=F(x)+C.\boxed{\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C}.∫f(x)dx=F(x)+C​.

Here fff is the integrand, dxdxdx names the variable, and CCC is any constant. The output is a family of functions, not one numerical area.

Why CCC? The derivatives of x2x^2x2, x2+3x^2+3x2+3, and x2−2x^2-2x2−2 are all 2x2x2x. Raising a graph by a constant changes its height but leaves every slope unchanged.

For example, ∫2x dx=x2+C\int2x\,dx=x^2+C∫2xdx=x2+C. If we also know F(0)=3F(0)=3F(0)=3, then C=3C=3C=3 and the family reduces to one member.

Important for JEE Main: differentiation is the final check. An answer is correct if its derivative equals the original integrand on the stated interval. Two different-looking answers can differ only by a constant on a connected interval.

Linearity is allowed:

∫(af+bg) dx=a∫f dx+b∫g dx\int(af+bg)\,dx=a\int f\,dx+b\int g\,dx∫(af+bg)dx=a∫fdx+b∫gdx

for constants a,ba,ba,b. But in general ∫fg≠(∫f)(∫g)\int fg\ne(\int f)(\int g)∫fg=(∫f)(∫g) and ∫(f/g)≠(∫f)/(∫g)\int(f/g)\ne(\int f)/(\int g)∫(f/g)=(∫f)/(∫g). For example, ∫x2dx=x3/3+C\int x^2dx=x^3/3+C∫x2dx=x3/3+C, whereas (∫xdx)2(\int xdx)^2(∫xdx)2 has the wrong derivative.

Concept C02 — Logs, absolute values and separate intervals

The real ln⁡x\ln xlnx is defined only for x>0x>0x>0. Yet 1/x1/x1/x exists for negative xxx too:

∫dxx=ln⁡∣x∣+C(x≠0).\boxed{\int\frac{dx}x=\ln|x|+C}\qquad(x\ne0).∫xdx​=ln∣x∣+C​(x=0).

For x<0x<0x<0, ln⁡∣x∣=ln⁡(−x)\ln|x|=\ln(-x)ln∣x∣=ln(−x) and its derivative is (−1)/(−x)=1/x(-1)/(-x)=1/x(−1)/(−x)=1/x. The absolute value makes the log input positive; it does not make the derivative positive.

The interval matters. A primitive can have one constant on (−∞,0)(-\infty,0)(−∞,0) and another on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞). There is no requirement to join across a point where the original function is undefined.

The useful pattern is

∫g′(x)g(x) dx=ln⁡∣g(x)∣+C\boxed{\int\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\,dx=\ln|g(x)|+C}∫g(x)g′(x)​dx=ln∣g(x)∣+C​

where g≠0g\ne0g=0 on the interval. For instance, ∫2x/(x2+3) dx=ln⁡(x2+3)+C\int2x/(x^2+3)\,dx=\ln(x^2+3)+C∫2x/(x2+3)dx=ln(x2+3)+C; here the inside is always positive.

Concept C04 — Substitution is the chain rule backwards

Suppose the integrand contains an inner expression g(x)g(x)g(x) and its derivative:

∫f(g(x))g′(x) dx.\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx.∫f(g(x))g′(x)dx.

Set u=g(x)u=g(x)u=g(x), so du=g′(x) dxdu=g'(x)\,dxdu=g′(x)dx. The integral becomes ∫f(u) du\int f(u)\,du∫f(u)du. After integrating, put uuu back.

Did you notice the matching pair?

∫2x1+x4 dx,u=x2,du=2x dx⇒∫du1+u2=tan⁡−1u+C.\int\frac{2x}{1+x^4}\,dx,\qquad u=x^2,\quad du=2x\,dx \quad\Rightarrow\quad \int\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\tan^{-1}u+C.∫1+x42x​dx,u=x2,du=2xdx⇒∫1+u2du​=tan−1u+C.

The fourth power becomes u2u^2u2, while 2x dx2x\,dx2xdx becomes exactly dududu. This is a useful substitution because it removes all the old xxx.

Bad route check: setting u=x4u=x^4u=x4 in ∫x/(1+x4)dx\int x/(1+x^4)dx∫x/(1+x4)dx leaves a factor x−2x^{-2}x−2 after forming dududu. It can be repaired, but it is longer. u=x2u=x^2u=x2 matches the numerator immediately.

Concept C05 — Reverse a product or quotient before using parts

Important for JEE Main. If you see exe^xex multiplying a function plus its derivative, the product rule is already present:

ddx(exg)=ex(g+g′)⇒∫ex(g+g′) dx=exg+C.\frac d{dx}(e^xg)=e^x(g+g') \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\int e^x(g+g')\,dx=e^xg+C}.dxd​(exg)=ex(g+g′)⇒∫ex(g+g′)dx=exg+C​.

More generally, ∫eax[g′+ag]dx=eaxg+C\int e^{ax}[g'+ag]dx=e^{ax}g+C∫eax[g′+ag]dx=eaxg+C. For g=sin⁡xg=\sin xg=sinx, this gives ∫ex(sin⁡x+cos⁡x)dx=exsin⁡x+C\int e^x(\sin x+\cos x)dx=e^x\sin x+C∫ex(sinx+cosx)dx=exsinx+C.

For a quotient:

ddxgh=hg′−gh′h2,h≠0.\frac d{dx}\frac{g}{h}=\frac{hg'-gh'}{h^2},\quad h\ne0.dxd​hg​=h2hg′−gh′​,h=0.

In Q3, ex(1/x−1/x2)e^x(1/x-1/x^2)ex(1/x−1/x2) is the derivative of ex/xe^x/xex/x. Separate integration by parts would create an integral that leads back to the original one. Seeing the combined derivative saves that loop.

Concept C06 — Integration by parts moves a derivative

Important for JEE Main. Start with the product rule: (uv)′=u′v+uv′(uv)'=u'v+uv'(uv)′=u′v+uv′. Rearrange and integrate:

∫u dv=uv−∫v du.\boxed{\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du}.∫udv=uv−∫vdu​.

Choose uuu so differentiation makes it simpler, and dvdvdv so its primitive is easy. The aim is a simpler new integral, not just a legal formula substitution.

ln⁡x\ln xlnx or inverse trig alone that function as uuu, dv=dxdv=dxdv=dx derivative becomes rational/algebraic
polynomial ×ln⁡x\times\ln x×lnx log as uuu often helps d(ln⁡x)=dx/xd(\ln x)=dx/xd(lnx)=dx/x cancels powers
exponential ×\times× trig parts twice if no combined derivative is visible the original integral returns; solve algebraically

Example:

∫xe2xdx=xe2x2−12∫e2xdx=e2x(x2−14)+C.\int xe^{2x}dx =\frac{xe^{2x}}2-\frac12\int e^{2x}dx =e^{2x}\left(\frac x2-\frac14\right)+C.∫xe2xdx=2xe2x​−21​∫e2xdx=e2x(2x​−41​)+C.

For a2+b2>0a^2+b^2>0a2+b2>0, the repeated-parts results are

∫eaxsin⁡bx dx=eax(asin⁡bx−bcos⁡bx)a2+b2+C,∫eaxcos⁡bx dx=eax(acos⁡bx+bsin⁡bx)a2+b2+C.\begin{aligned} \int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx&= \frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx-b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C,\\ \int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx&= \frac{e^{ax}(a\cos bx+b\sin bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C. \end{aligned}∫eaxsinbxdx∫eaxcosbxdx​=a2+b2eax(asinbx−bcosbx)​+C,=a2+b2eax(acosbx+bsinbx)​+C.​

Use these after checking the combined-derivative pattern first. A mnemonic for choosing uuu is only a hint, not a law.

Concept C07 — Trig integrals: keep a derivative factor

Important for JEE Main. Do not integrate a power by blindly raising the power again. For example, (tan⁡4x/4)′=tan⁡3xsec⁡2x(\tan^4x/4)'=\tan^3x\sec^2x(tan4x/4)′=tan3xsec2x, which has an extra factor.

Use the identities

sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1,sec⁡2x=1+tan⁡2x,csc⁡2x=1+cot⁡2x.\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1,\quad \sec^2x=1+\tan^2x,\quad \csc^2x=1+\cot^2x.sin2x+cos2x=1,sec2x=1+tan2x,csc2x=1+cot2x.

Both sine/cosine powers even sin⁡2x=(1−cos⁡2x)/2\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2sin2x=(1−cos2x)/2, cos⁡2x=(1+cos⁡2x)/2\cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2cos2x=(1+cos2x)/2

Concept C08 — Partial fractions undo a combined denominator

Important for JEE Main. A rational function is a polynomial divided by another polynomial. If the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree, first divide. Then split a proper fraction into pieces we can integrate.

x+5(x+1)(x+3)=Ax+1+Bx+3.\frac{x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)} =\frac A{x+1}+\frac B{x+3}.(x+1)(x+3)x+5​=x+1A​+x+3B​.

Multiplying by the denominator gives an identity:

x+5=A(x+3)+B(x+1).x+5=A(x+3)+B(x+1).x+5=A(x+3)+B(x+1).

Choose x=−1x=-1x=−1 to isolate A=2A=2A=2 and x=−3x=-3x=−3 to isolate B=−1B=-1B=−1. We use those values in the polynomial identity, not as inputs in the original undefined fraction.

Then integrate the simpler terms as logs. The original exclusions x=−1,−3x=-1,-3x=−1,−3 stay excluded.

Templates worth remembering:

P(x)(x−a)(x−b)=Ax−a+Bx−b,a≠b,P(x)(x−a)2=Ax−a+B(x−a)2after polynomial division if needed,P(x)(x−a)(x2+px+q)=Ax−a+Bx+Cx2+px+q\begin{aligned} \frac{P(x)}{(x-a)(x-b)}&=\frac A{x-a}+\frac B{x-b},\quad a\ne b,\\ \frac{P(x)}{(x-a)^2}&=\frac A{x-a}+\frac B{(x-a)^2} \quad\text{after polynomial division if needed},\\ \frac{P(x)}{(x-a)(x^2+px+q)} &=\frac A{x-a}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+px+q} \end{aligned}(x−a)(x−b)P(x)​(x−a)2P(x)​(x−a)(x2+px+q)P(x)​​=x−aA​+x−bB​,a=b,=x−aA​+(x−a)2B​after polynomial division if needed,=x−aA​+x2+px+qBx+C​​

for a real irreducible quadratic in the last row. Include every repeated power, and use a linear numerator over a quadratic. Determine coefficients by an identity, not by guessing from the integrals.

Concept C09 — Complete the square before deciding “log or inverse tan”

For a quadratic q(x)=ax2+bx+cq(x)=ax^2+bx+cq(x)=ax2+bx+c, a≠0a\ne0a=0:

q=a[(x+b2a)2+4ac−b24a2].q=a\left[\left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2+ \frac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}\right].q=a[(x+2ab​)2+4a24ac−b2​].

After shifting the input, a sum of squares gives inverse tangent; a difference of squares gives logs via partial fractions. A perfect square gives a power integral.

If the numerator is Mx+NMx+NMx+N, first match the denominator derivative:

Mx+N=M2a(2ax+b)+(N−Mb2a).Mx+N=\frac{M}{2a}(2ax+b)+ \left(N-\frac{Mb}{2a}\right).Mx+N=2aM​(2ax+b)+(N−2aMb​).

The first part integrates to (M/2a)ln⁡∣q∣(M/2a)\ln|q|(M/2a)ln∣q∣; the constant part uses the completed-square standard form.

Reciprocal quartic clue: for Q6 divide numerator and denominator by x2x^2x2 on x≠0x\ne0x=0:

x2+1x4+1=1+x−2x2+x−2=1+x−2(x−x−1)2+2.\frac{x^2+1}{x^4+1} =\frac{1+x^{-2}}{x^2+x^{-2}} =\frac{1+x^{-2}}{(x-x^{-1})^2+2}.x4+1x2+1​=x2+x−21+x−2​=(x−x−1)2+21+x−2​.

Now u=x−1/xu=x-1/xu=x−1/x has exactly the required derivative 1+1/x21+1/x^21+1/x2. Notice the minus in uuu: differentiating −1/x-1/x−1/x gives a plus. We will separately check the missing input 000 before claiming an all-real answer.

For the circular radical, the point (x,1−x2)(x,\sqrt{1-x^2})(x,1−x2​) lies on the upper unit semicircle. If x=sin⁡θx=\sin\thetax=sinθ on the principal interval, the other triangle side is cos⁡θ≥0\cos\theta\ge0cosθ≥0.

Then

∫1−x2 dx=∫cos⁡2θ dθ=12(θ+sin⁡θcos⁡θ)+C.\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx =\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta =\frac12(\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta)+C.∫1−x2​dx=∫cos2θdθ=21​(θ+sinθcosθ)+C.

Putting the original variable back gives [x1−x2+sin⁡−1x]/2+C[x\sqrt{1-x^2}+\sin^{-1}x]/2+C[x1−x2​+sin−1x]/2+C.

Standard radical primitives for a>0a>0a>0:

∫a2−x2 dx=12[xa2−x2+a2sin⁡−1xa]+C,∫x2+a2 dx=12[xx2+a2+a2ln⁡∣x+x2+a2∣]+C,∫x2−a2 dx=12[xx2−a2−a2ln⁡∣x+x2−a2∣]+C.\begin{aligned} \int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx &=\frac12\left[x\sqrt{a^2-x^2} +a^2\sin^{-1}\frac xa\right]+C,\\ \int\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\,dx &=\frac12\left[x\sqrt{x^2+a^2} +a^2\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right|\right]+C,\\ \int\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\,dx &=\frac12\left[x\sqrt{x^2-a^2} -a^2\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right|\right]+C. \end{aligned}∫a2−x2​dx∫x2+a2​dx∫x2−a2​dx​=21​[xa2−x2​+a2sin−1ax​]+C,=21​[xx2+a2​+a2ln​x+x2+a2​​]+C,=21​[xx2−a2​−a2ln​x+x2−a2​​]+C.​

Use their real interior domains; endpoint values may be obtained by continuity where finite. The signs in front of the log follow the sign under the radical.

General quadratic radicals — Important for JEE Main. The syllabus also lists 1/ax2+bx+c1/\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}1/ax2+bx+c​ and (Mx+N)/ax2+bx+c(Mx+N)/\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}(Mx+N)/ax2+bx+c​. Do not memorize each shifted version separately.

For q(x)=ax2+bx+cq(x)=ax^2+bx+cq(x)=ax2+bx+c, a≠0a\ne0a=0, work on an interval where q>0q>0q>0. Match its derivative:

Mx+N=M2a(2ax+b)+(N−Mb2a).Mx+N=\frac M{2a}(2ax+b)+ \left(N-\frac{Mb}{2a}\right).Mx+N=2aM​(2ax+b)+(N−2aMb​).

Since (q)′=q′/(2q)(\sqrt q)'=q'/(2\sqrt q)(q​)′=q′/(2q​),

∫Mx+Nq dx=Maq+(N−Mb2a)∫dxq.\boxed{ \int\frac{Mx+N}{\sqrt q}\,dx =\frac Ma\sqrt q+ \left(N-\frac{Mb}{2a}\right)\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt q}}.∫q​Mx+N​dx=aM​q​+(N−2aMb​)∫q​dx​​.

Include the final +C+C+C after evaluating the remaining integral. Complete the square in that integral, then use the standard sum/difference radical rows from C03. For example,

∫dx−x2+4x+5=∫dx9−(x−2)2=sin⁡−1x−23+C,−1<x<5,∫dx2x2+4x+6=12∫dx(x+1)2+2=12ln⁡(x+1+(x+1)2+2)+C.\begin{aligned} \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{-x^2+4x+5}} &=\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-(x-2)^2}} =\sin^{-1}\frac{x-2}3+C,\quad -1<x<5,\\ \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2x^2+4x+6}} &=\frac1{\sqrt2}\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x+1)^2+2}}\\ &=\frac1{\sqrt2}\ln\left(x+1+\sqrt{(x+1)^2+2}\right)+C. \end{aligned}∫−x2+4x+5​dx​∫2x2+4x+6​dx​​=∫9−(x−2)2​dx​=sin−13x−2​+C,−1<x<5,=2​1​∫(x+1)2+2​dx​=2​1​ln(x+1+(x+1)2+2​)+C.​

For ∫ax2+bx+c dx\int\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}\,dx∫ax2+bx+c​dx, the same shift and scale reduce it to one of the three radical primitives above. If a=0a=0a=0, the inside is linear and u=bx+cu=bx+cu=bx+c is simpler. Always determine the real interval before taking a square root outside a factor.

Concept C11 — Simplify roots or combine trig waves first

Conjugate clue: with x+1+x\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt xx+1​+x​ below the fraction, multiply by the difference:

1x+1+x=x+1−x(x+1)−x=x+1−x.\frac1{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt x} =\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt x}{(x+1)-x} =\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt x.x+1​+x​1​=(x+1)−xx+1​−x​​=x+1​−x​.

Now ordinary power integration is enough. Expanding a power series here would be much longer and would introduce a convergence question that we do not need.

Shifted-wave clue: write

Acos⁡x+Bsin⁡x=Rcos⁡(x−ϕ),R=A2+B2>0,A\cos x+B\sin x=R\cos(x-\phi),\quad R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}>0,Acosx+Bsinx=Rcos(x−ϕ),R=A2+B2​>0,

where Rcos⁡ϕ=AR\cos\phi=ARcosϕ=A, Rsin⁡ϕ=BR\sin\phi=BRsinϕ=B. A reciprocal then becomes a scaled secant integral. This is simpler than the general half-angle substitution when the denominator is just one linear combination.

For a more general rational expression in sin⁡x,cos⁡x\sin x,\cos xsinx,cosx, set t=tan⁡(x/2)t=\tan(x/2)t=tan(x/2):

sin⁡x=2t1+t2,cos⁡x=1−t21+t2,dx=2 dt1+t2.\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\quad \cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\quad dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}.sinx=1+t22t​,cosx=1+t21−t2​,dx=1+t22dt​.

It converts the problem into a rational integral. Use it on intervals where the substitution is defined; x=(2k+1)πx=(2k+1)\pix=(2k+1)π is a break of this coordinate formula even when the original integrand is finite there. A shorter identity or derivative match should be tried first.

For rational powers such as x1/2x^{1/2}x1/2 and x1/3x^{1/3}x1/3 together on x>0x>0x>0, x=t6x=t^6x=t6 can remove both fractional powers. For a lone ax+b\sqrt{ax+b}ax+b​, t=ax+bt=\sqrt{ax+b}t=ax+b​ may help. The substitution must simplify the entire integrand, including dxdxdx.

Concept C12 — A primitive formula can have a branch jump

Inverse trig functions return principal angles. They do not automatically join through every input introduced by a substitution.

In Q6 the original function is positive and continuous for all real xxx, so any all-real primitive should be smooth and increasing. The printed expression

P(x)=12tan⁡−1(x2−12 x)P(x)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x^2-1}{\sqrt2\,x}\right)P(x)=2​1​tan−1(2​xx2−1​)

has a jump at 000. Its derivative is correct on each side, but the formula alone is not an all-real primitive.

A globally smooth alternative is

G(x)=12[tan⁡−1(2x+1)+tan⁡−1(2x−1)].G(x)=\frac1{\sqrt2} \left[\tan^{-1}(\sqrt2x+1)+\tan^{-1}(\sqrt2x-1)\right].G(x)=2​1​[tan−1(2​x+1)+tan−1(2​x−1)].

Its derivative is the original integrand at every real input. The solution shows the algebra. The lesson is useful beyond this question: check the original domain and the transformed formula's domain separately.

For Q11, sec⁡−1x\sec^{-1}xsec−1x has positive derivative on both x>1x>1x>1 and x<−1x<-1x<−1, whereas 1/[xx2−1]1/[x\sqrt{x^2-1}]1/[xx2−1​] is negative on x<−1x<-1x<−1. A safe primitive is sec⁡−1∣x∣\sec^{-1}|x|sec−1∣x∣, or tan⁡−1x2−1\tan^{-1}\sqrt{x^2-1}tan−1x2−1​, on the two separate intervals.

Concept C13 — Given answer forms and initial values can save work

Important for JEE Main. If a question gives a proposed answer with unknown coefficients, differentiate it and compare with the original integrand.

For Q14:

ddx[ex2(ax2+b)]=ex2[2ax3+2(a+b)x].\frac d{dx}\left[e^{x^2}(ax^2+b)\right] =e^{x^2}\left[2ax^3+2(a+b)x\right].dxd​[ex2(ax2+b)]=ex2[2ax3+2(a+b)x].

To equal x3ex2x^3e^{x^2}x3ex2, match 2a=12a=12a=1 and a+b=0a+b=0a+b=0. This is a usable alternative to doing substitution and parts.

If a condition gives F(a)=bF(a)=bF(a)=b, first find F=G+CF=G+CF=G+C, then C=b−G(a)C=b-G(a)C=b−G(a). Do not put C=0C=0C=0 just because the given value is zero; G(a)G(a)G(a) may not be zero.

Last-minute formula recap

∫xndx=xn+1n+1+C (n≠−1),∫g′gdx=ln⁡∣g∣+C,∫f(g)g′ dx=F(g)+C(F′=f),∫u dv=uv−∫v du,∫eax(g′+ag) dx=eaxg+C,∫dxa2+x2=1atan⁡−1xa+C,∫dxa2−x2=sin⁡−1xa+C,∫sec⁡x dx=ln⁡∣sec⁡x+tan⁡x∣+C,∫tan⁡x dx=−ln⁡∣cos⁡x∣+C.\begin{gathered} \int x^n dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\ (n\ne-1),\qquad \int\frac{g'}g dx=\ln|g|+C,\\ \int f(g)g'\,dx=F(g)+C\quad(F'=f),\qquad \int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du,\\ \int e^{ax}(g'+ag)\,dx=e^{ax}g+C,\\ \int\frac{dx}{a^2+x^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa+C,\quad \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\frac xa+C,\\ \int\sec x\,dx=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C,\qquad \int\tan x\,dx=-\ln|\cos x|+C. \end{gathered}∫xndx=n+1xn+1​+C (n=−1),∫gg′​dx=ln∣g∣+C,∫f(g)g′dx=F(g)+C(F′=f),∫udv=uv−∫vdu,∫eax(g′+ag)dx=eaxg+C,∫a2+x2dx​=a1​tan−1ax​+C,∫a2−x2​dx​=sin−1ax​+C,∫secxdx=ln∣secx+tanx∣+C,∫tanxdx=−ln∣cosx∣+C.​

Here a>0a>0a>0 and all domain conditions from the full tables still apply. Remember the power, exponential and trig primitive table in C03 and the three radical formulas in C10.

Final check: differentiate; check inner factors; keep +C+C+C; keep excluded points; and use the given value only after finding the general primitive.

Worked solutions to the 20 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Complete the square to expose a standard integral

PDF page 60 | MCQ | Notes: C03,C09

∫dxx2+4x+13\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+4x+13}∫x2+4x+13dx​ equals

  • (a) 12tan⁡−1(x+22)+C\frac12\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}2\right)+C21​tan−1(2x+2​)+C
  • (b) tan⁡−1(x+2)+C\tan^{-1}(x+2)+Ctan−1(x+2)+C
  • (c) 13tan⁡−1(x+23)+C\frac13\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}3\right)+C31​tan−1(3x+2​)+C
  • (d) 13tan⁡−1(x+29)+C\frac13\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}9\right)+C31​tan−1(9x+2​)+C

Did you notice a quadratic below a constant numerator? First ask whether it can become a sum of squares:

x2+4x+13=(x+2)2+9.x^2+4x+13=(x+2)^2+9.x2+4x+13=(x+2)2+9.

Put u=x+2u=x+2u=x+2, du=dxdu=dxdu=dx. Then

∫duu2+32=13tan⁡−1x+23+C(c).\int\frac{du}{u^2+3^2} =\boxed{\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac{x+2}3+C}\quad\text{(c)}.∫u2+32du​=31​tan−13x+2​+C​(c).

Check the scale: differentiating gives 131/31+(x+2)2/9=1/[(x+2)2+9]\frac13\frac{1/3}{1+(x+2)^2/9}=1/[(x+2)^2+9]31​1+(x+2)2/91/3​=1/[(x+2)2+9]. The two factors of 1/31/31/3 have different jobs: one is outside the primitive; one comes from differentiating the inside.

Question 2 — See the product rule backwards

PDF page 60 | MCQ | Notes: C05

∫ex(sin⁡x+cos⁡x) dx\displaystyle\int e^x(\sin x+\cos x)\,dx∫ex(sinx+cosx)dx equals

  • (a) exsin⁡x+Ce^x\sin x+Cexsinx+C
  • (b) excos⁡x+Ce^x\cos x+Cexcosx+C
  • (c) ex(sin⁡x−cos⁡x)+Ce^x(\sin x-\cos x)+Cex(sinx−cosx)+C
  • (d) exsin⁡x2+C\dfrac{e^x\sin x}2+C2exsinx​+C

This is already a product derivative. Did you notice that the derivative of sin⁡x\sin xsinx is the other term, cos⁡x\cos xcosx?

ddx(exsin⁡x)=exsin⁡x+excos⁡x.\frac d{dx}(e^x\sin x) =e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x.dxd​(exsinx)=exsinx+excosx.

Therefore ∫ex(sin⁡x+cos⁡x) dx=exsin⁡x+C\boxed{\int e^x(\sin x+\cos x)\,dx=e^x\sin x+C}∫ex(sinx+cosx)dx=exsinx+C​, (a), for all real xxx.

Another possible approach: integrate the sine term by parts: ∫exsin⁡x=exsin⁡x−∫excos⁡x\int e^x\sin x=e^x\sin x-\int e^x\cos x∫exsinx=exsinx−∫excosx. The remaining cosine integral cancels the original cosine term. The reverse-product view sees that cancellation before calculating.

Question 3 — A quotient derivative is already present

PDF page 60 | MCQ | Notes: C05

∫ex(1x−1x2) dx\displaystyle\int e^x\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x^2}\right)\,dx∫ex(x1​−x21​)dx equals

  • (a) exln⁡x+Ce^x\ln x+Cexlnx+C
  • (b) −exx+C-\dfrac{e^x}x+C−xex​+C
  • (c) exx2+C\dfrac{e^x}{x^2}+Cx2ex​+C
  • (d) exx+C\dfrac{e^x}x+Cxex​+C

Read the two terms as one derivative pattern. The derivative of 1/x1/x1/x is −1/x2-1/x^2−1/x2, so

ddx(ex1x)=ex(1x−1x2).\frac d{dx}\left(e^x\frac1x\right) =e^x\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x^2}\right).dxd​(exx1​)=ex(x1​−x21​).

Thus ex/x+C\boxed{e^x/x+C}ex/x+C​, (d), on an interval with x≠0x\ne0x=0.

Another possible view: the quotient rule gives (ex/x)′=(xex−ex)/x2(e^x/x)'=(xe^x-e^x)/x^2(ex/x)′=(xex−ex)/x2, exactly the same integrand. Splitting and trying parts repeatedly is possible but hides the cancellation. Keep the two terms together.

Question 4 — Integration by parts removes the polynomial factor

PDF page 60 | MCQ | Notes: C06

∫xe2x dx\displaystyle\int xe^{2x}\,dx∫xe2xdx equals

  • (a) e2x(x2+14)+Ce^{2x}\left(\frac x2+\frac14\right)+Ce2x(2x​+41​)+C
  • (b) e2x(x2−14)+Ce^{2x}\left(\frac x2-\frac14\right)+Ce2x(2x​−41​)+C
  • (c) e2x(x−1)+Ce^{2x}(x-1)+Ce2x(x−1)+C
  • (d) x2e2x4+C\dfrac{x^2e^{2x}}4+C4x2e2x​+C

The factor xxx becomes simpler when differentiated. Use parts with u=xu=xu=x, dv=e2xdxdv=e^{2x}dxdv=e2xdx. Then du=dxdu=dxdu=dx and v=e2x/2v=e^{2x}/2v=e2x/2.

I=xe2x2−12∫e2xdx=e2x(x2−14)+C(b).\begin{aligned} I&=\frac{xe^{2x}}2-\frac12\int e^{2x}dx\\ &=\boxed{e^{2x}\left(\frac x2-\frac14\right)+C} \quad\text{(b)}. \end{aligned}I​=2xe2x​−21​∫e2xdx=e2x(2x​−41​)+C​(b).​

Another possible approach — use the answer's shape. Try e2x(Ax+B)e^{2x}(Ax+B)e2x(Ax+B). Its derivative is e2x[2Ax+(2B+A)]e^{2x}[2Ax+(2B+A)]e2x[2Ax+(2B+A)]. Matching xe2xxe^{2x}xe2x gives A=1/2A=1/2A=1/2, B=−1/4B=-1/4B=−1/4. Both routes are short; parts is the general reusable method.

Question 5 — Save a tangent derivative by using an identity

PDF page 60 | MCQ | Notes: C07

∫tan⁡3x dx\displaystyle\int\tan^3x\,dx∫tan3xdx equals

  • (a) tan⁡2x2−ln⁡∣cos⁡x∣+C\dfrac{\tan^2x}2-\ln|\cos x|+C2tan2x​−ln∣cosx∣+C
  • (b) tan⁡2x2+ln⁡∣cos⁡x∣+C\dfrac{\tan^2x}2+\ln|\cos x|+C2tan2x​+ln∣cosx∣+C
  • (c) tan⁡4x4+C\dfrac{\tan^4x}4+C4tan4x​+C
  • (d) sec⁡2x2+ln⁡∣sin⁡x∣+C\dfrac{\sec^2x}2+\ln|\sin x|+C2sec2x​+ln∣sinx∣+C

Why not write tan⁡4x/4\tan^4x/4tan4x/4? Differentiating it gives tan⁡3xsec⁡2x\tan^3x\sec^2xtan3xsec2x, with an extra factor absent from the question.

Save a known derivative by writing

tan⁡3x=tan⁡x(sec⁡2x−1).\tan^3x=\tan x(\sec^2x-1).tan3x=tanx(sec2x−1).

Then

∫tan⁡3x dx=∫tan⁡xsec⁡2x dx−∫tan⁡x dx=tan⁡2x2+ln⁡∣cos⁡x∣+C(b).\int\tan^3x\,dx =\int\tan x\sec^2x\,dx-\int\tan x\,dx =\boxed{\frac{\tan^2x}2+\ln|\cos x|+C} \quad\text{(b)}.∫tan3xdx=∫tanxsec2xdx−∫tanxdx=2tan2x​+ln∣cosx∣+C​(b).

For the first term use u=tan⁡xu=\tan xu=tanx; for the second use the standard tangent primitive. Work on intervals where cos⁡x≠0\cos x\ne0cosx=0.

Question 6 — The reciprocal substitution works on separate intervals

PDF page 60 | MCQ | Notes: C04,C09,C12

∫x2+1x4+1 dx\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+1}{x^4+1}\,dx∫x4+1x2+1​dx equals

  • (a) 12tan⁡−1(x2+12 x)+C\dfrac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^2+1}{\sqrt2\,x}\right)+C2​1​tan−1(2​xx2+1​)+C
  • (b) tan⁡−1(x2−1x)+C\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^2-1}x\right)+Ctan−1(xx2−1​)+C
  • (c) 12ln⁡∣x2−1x2+1∣+C\dfrac12\ln\left|\dfrac{x^2-1}{x^2+1}\right|+C21​ln​x2+1x2−1​​+C
  • (d) 12tan⁡−1(x2−12 x)+C\dfrac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^2-1}{\sqrt2\,x}\right)+C2​1​tan−1(2​xx2−1​)+C

First notice the reciprocal structure. A direct u=x2u=x^2u=x2 would not match the numerator x2+1x^2+1x2+1. Instead, on x≠0x\ne0x=0, divide top and bottom by x2x^2x2:

I=∫1+x−2x2+x−2 dx=∫1+x−2(x−x−1)2+2 dx.I=\int\frac{1+x^{-2}}{x^2+x^{-2}}\,dx =\int\frac{1+x^{-2}}{(x-x^{-1})^2+2}\,dx.I=∫x2+x−21+x−2​dx=∫(x−x−1)2+21+x−2​dx.

Good, the derivative of x−1/xx-1/xx−1/x is precisely 1+1/x21+1/x^21+1/x2. Let u=x−1/xu=x-1/xu=x−1/x:

I=∫duu2+2=12tan⁡−1x2−12 x+C.I=\int\frac{du}{u^2+2} =\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x^2-1}{\sqrt2\,x}+C.I=∫u2+2du​=2​1​tan−12​xx2−1​+C.

This is the intended option (d), separately on x>0x>0x>0 or on x<0x<0x<0.

Source qualification: the original integrand has no real denominator zero, including at x=0x=0x=0. But the printed expression has limits

lim⁡x→0−P(x)=π22,lim⁡x→0+P(x)=−π22.\lim_{x\to0^-}P(x)=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2},\qquad \lim_{x\to0^+}P(x)=-\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}.x→0−lim​P(x)=22​π​,x→0+lim​P(x)=−22​π​.

One single added constant cannot remove that jump.

Another possible approach — an all-real primitive. The identity

x2+1x4+1=12[1x2+2x+1+1x2−2x+1]\frac{x^2+1}{x^4+1} =\frac12\left[ \frac1{x^2+\sqrt2x+1}+ \frac1{x^2-\sqrt2x+1}\right]x4+1x2+1​=21​[x2+2​x+11​+x2−2​x+11​]

follows by adding the fractions; their denominator product is x4+1x^4+1x4+1. Completing the square in each gives

G(x)=12[tan⁡−1(2x+1)+tan⁡−1(2x−1)]+C.\boxed{G(x)=\frac1{\sqrt2} \left[\tan^{-1}(\sqrt2x+1)+\tan^{-1}(\sqrt2x-1)\right]+C}.G(x)=2​1​[tan−1(2​x+1)+tan−1(2​x−1)]+C​.

Its derivative equals the original integrand for every real xxx. The reciprocal substitution is shorter for choosing the intended MCQ option; the split-quadratic route also handles the missing input honestly.

Question 7 — Split before expanding a cubic denominator

PDF page 61 | MCQ | Notes: C05,C08

∫dxx(x3+1)\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x(x^3+1)}∫x(x3+1)dx​ equals

  • (a) 13ln⁡∣x3x3+1∣+C\dfrac13\ln\left|\dfrac{x^3}{x^3+1}\right|+C31​ln​x3+1x3​​+C
  • (b) 13ln⁡∣x3+1x3∣+C\dfrac13\ln\left|\dfrac{x^3+1}{x^3}\right|+C31​ln​x3x3+1​​+C
  • (c) ln⁡∣x∣+ln⁡∣x3+1∣+C\ln|x|+\ln|x^3+1|+Cln∣x∣+ln∣x3+1∣+C
